The film's a legend: Cecil B De Mille actually played himself. This Lloyd Webber musical (book and lyrics by Don Black and Christopher Hampton) had an outing with Glenn Close at ENO a while back, and this is Jamie Lloyd's ultra-moody, mixed-media monochrome take on it.
Lloyd’s streamlined approach has a power of its own.
By the end, for all its technical dazzlement, you’re left thinking, have we been watching “Sunset Boulevard” or “Everybody’s Talking About Jamie Lloyd”?
Overall the show feels like a Gothic opera staged in an underground car park during a blackout.

Any actor in a Jamie Lloyd show – the public face of the creative vision – have to put a great deal of of faith in the director’s decision-making and trust the cohesive direction of the production. And it is a faith that pays off almost every time, eliciting unexpected and powerfully alchemical performances from his casts.

Sunset Boulevard never really gels as a whole.
The revival, directed by Jamie Lloyd, took a daringly austere approach, forgoing grand stage machinery in favor of a largely monochrome scheme.

Lloyd, who is known for his innovative work across recent adaptations of The Seagull, A Doll’s House and Cyrano de Bergerac, as well as the National Theatre’s The Effect, certainly provides blue sky thinking for how theatre can incorporate film technology in new ways. It’s exciting to think what he may have next.
This production is unique, exciting, and stretches the boundaries of what we believe can be achieved in theatre... this is a show you cannot miss.

Literally black-and-white (like the 1950. Billy Wilder film on which the musical is based) until its blood-splattered denouement, the production is a stunner. If little about the Evita rejig made sense, everything here is in service to the story.

cn.t: Jamie Lloyd's audacious, stripped-back reimagining divides critics, but Scherzinger's star turn wins widespread praise. The stark, film-noir aesthetic and innovative camera work dazzle some while feeling gimmicky to others.
